doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Impact of the civil rights movement on his life
summary: He says it barely changed his career, recalls riding segregated buses in Memphis, and urges young people to take advantage of opportunities.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What was the impact of the civil rights movement and then the civil rights bill in ’64 or whatever. Did it make any difference in your life?

To tell you the truth I can’t say that it did really. The only thing it could have made a difference was that maybe hotel accommodations or something, but see I didn’t really get caught up in that because the real troopers like the Dinah Washingtons and the Harry Belafonte and people like that, they were the ones who really suffered with that where they could work at a club in any city but they couldn’t stay at the hotel where they worked, or they had to change their clothes in the bus or something. So I really kind of avoided it but I can’t say that it enhanced my career one way of the other. But I’ve always been down for the cause naturally, right is right and wrong is wrong, you know. Because when I was in Memphis, Tennessee the buses I used to board you’d have to sit in the back of the bus. When we got on the bus even then, and we weren’t trying to be militants we just knew that this is wrong. Here’s all these seats here, I got to go to the back of the bus and maybe get a seat or stand up. So we would just sit there and they’d say — and this is no lie — he’d say “boy” (this was his exact words, and I’d say, you did say “Roy” didn’t you) then he’d say, “Get in the back of the bus.” And we would get up and go towards the back of the bus. But every day they would have to tell us to do it. We would just sit down. You know like the freedom fighter lady, you know what I’m talking about, I must be losing it I can’t think of it off the top of my head.

But anyway that’s the way it was. But I have great respect for all the people involved with it because all the people, all races, gave up a lot to make things better. That’s why when I look at some of these young people out here acting like fools and dressing like clowns it bothers me that everything — here you’ve got a black president of the United States and you would think you would be so motivated but they’re not. It’s like they go on worse. You know it makes no sense. There’s been a lot of people to give up things, their lives, to make it better for you to go to school, to get a scholarship, like you were saying, even the jazz students here. You’ve got a chance to go to school to learn how to play jazz. Even when I was going to high school jazz was halfway tolerated. “Oh that’s enough of that jazz, let’s play these marches.” But now you can go to school to learn how
to play jazz and a lot of them don’t even take advantage of that. It makes no sense you see what I’m saying. Oh Rosa Parks.
